strengths: Well-motivated systematic approach: Clear empirical justification for identifying projection layer as task-synergy memory through principled comparison in Table 1
Novel HEE-based NAS strategy: Creative hierarchical exploration-exploitation sampling using CLS token similarity; clearly outperforms pure exploration (6% improvement in Table 4)
Strong empirical results: 83.44% on VDD (3.3% above L2P), 94.82% on 5-Datasets; consistent improvements across multiple baselines
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple random seeds, extensive ablations (component selection, Adapt implementations, task orders), released code
Interpretable learned structures: Figure 4 demonstrates sensible task synergies (similar tasks reuse, dissimilar tasks adapt), providing transparency into model decisions
Excellent presentation and clarity: Well-written with clear figures and thorough appendix with implementation details and hyperparameters
weaknesses: Critical limitation to task-incremental setting: Requires task ID at inference, limiting practical applicability; preliminary attempts to enable class-incremental learning mentioned but dismissed without sufficient exploration (Section 3.3)

Generalization concerns for CHEEM identification: Component selection validated only on VDD via sequential fine-tuning without forgetting mechanisms; unclear if projection layer is optimal across different benchmarks, domains, or ViT architectures (only ViT-B/8 tested)

Scalability issues: 1.06M parameters per task accumulate to ~53M for 50 tasks; significant variance in per-task parameter growth (0.296M to 2.365M) across task orders; evaluation only on 10-task and 5-task benchmarks

Fairness in baseline comparisons: CHEEM updates backbone while L2P/S-Prompts freeze it (different capacity); SupSup/EFT/LL modifications for ViTs may not be optimal; L2G applied only to projection layer rather than uniformly; missing comparisons with recent methods (DualPrompt)
Task order sensitivity: Performance ranges 82.06%-83.74% (>1.5% variance, Table 13), indicating robustness concerns despite claims of stability

Limited ablation of HEE strategy: Normalized cosine similarity (Eq. 4) uses data-dependent min/max normalization that shifts as experts are added (potential instability); auxiliary expert score (Eq. 5) ad-hoc; only PE vs. HEE compared, no ablation on similarity metrics or sampling levels
Missing computational analysis: No training time comparison, memory footprint during NAS, or runtime overhead relative to baselines
Lack of theoretical justification: Purely empirical work with no formal analysis of why task-similarity-based sampling should improve plasticity-stability trade-off or convergence guarantees

strengths: Well-articulated problem formulation with clear taxonomy of ExfCCL design choices (benchmarks, backbone adaptation, head design, capacity), providing valuable framing for the community
Intuitive four-operation framework (Reuse, Adapt, New, Skip) with clear distinction from prior work L2G; sensible task-tailored architectures learned and interpretable

Comprehensive experimental evaluation on two challenging realistic benchmarks (MTIL, VDD) with varying class distributions, both Tiny and Base ViTs, extensive baselines, and thorough ablations (HEE vs uniform, component placement, hyperparameter sensitivity, task order robustness)
Strong empirical results with substantial FoM improvements over all baselines and close approach to full fine-tuning upper bounds (85.9% vs 88.1% MTIL ViT-Base); particularly strong on DEiT-Tiny
Insightful theoretical analysis explaining local vs. global argmax discrepancy (Section I, Table 19) that elegantly accounts for baseline failures; systematic component identification via ablation
Thorough reproducibility support with implementation details, hyperparameters, code promise, and multiple runs with error bars; generalization demonstrated on CLIP ViT-Base
weaknesses: Limited novelty in individual components: relies on existing SPOS for supernet construction, straightforward CLS-token cosine similarity for task comparison, and standard hierarchical sampling; main contribution is combination of techniques for continual learning rather than fundamental algorithmic innovation

Significant computational overhead and complexity: three-stage pipeline (supernet construction, evolutionary search, finetuning) requires ~1.45h/task on A100 (higher than several baselines); FLOPs nearly doubled due to task ID inference requirement; requires careful hyperparameter tuning (ε₁, ε₂, τ) with non-trivial sensitivity

Task ID inference dependency undermines task-agnostic claims: requires external task-centroid memory and initial backbone forward pass; CHEEMlite partially mitigates but doesn't eliminate this requirement; limited analysis of task ID inference failure modes and their impact

Limited evaluation scope: only two benchmarks both in image classification; maximum 12 tasks tested; unclear scalability to longer task streams (50+ tasks) or significant domain shifts; practical applicability concerns due to method complexity

Insufficient analysis of learned dynamic architectures: Figures 3 and 6 show examples but lack systematic investigation of why operations are chosen, consistency across runs, and temporal stability of architectures as new tasks arrive

Technical presentation issues: main algorithm expressed through figures rather than clear pseudocode; notation inconsistencies (superscript/subscript usage); related work could better position against recent continual learning methods; Section I analysis somewhat disconnected from main narrative
